notes:
I couldn't run every search I planned, so some verses have thin notes. The sources I read mostly give one shared evangelical reading. They didn't show the Protestant traditions disagreeing sharply on this chapter. The few real disagreements are marked **[Differing views]**.

---

**v. 1: The angel of the LORD; from Gilgal to Bochim**
- **Who the angel is (traditional view):** Guzik (Enduring Word) thinks this is probably God himself in human form, and specifically the pre-incarnate Christ. His reasons: the speaker claims to have led Israel out of Egypt and made the covenant, and the invisible Father would not appear in a body. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-2/
- MacArthur calls it one of three appearances of the pre-incarnate Christ in Judges. Lindsey (Bible Knowledge Commentary) agrees: the second Person of the Trinity in visible form, not just an angel. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_commentary
- Maclaren says the angel's repeated "I" only makes sense if he is the one who is distinct from Jehovah yet one with him, whom we know as the Word made flesh. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_notes
- Grant says this is *the* messenger, the Lord himself, not just *a* messenger. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/judges-2.html
- **[Differing views] on the angel:** Guzik admits it's fair to ask whether every "angel of the LORD" is God appearing. He quotes G. Campbell Morgan, who says the speaker may have been a prophet, since the word can equally mean "messenger." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-2/
- Moore's critical commentary, from modern scholarship, says the messenger is not a prophet but, as always in Judges, Yahweh himself appearing to people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/angel_of_the_lord
- **The place names:** The HCSB note contrasts the two movements. Israel failed to "go up" against the Canaanites, so the Angel "went up" against Israel. Gilgal was Israel's first camp in the land, where they set up memorial stones and kept Passover. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_commentary
- The Biblical Illustrator sums it up: Gilgal is named for what God did, Bochim for what the people felt. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/2-3.html
- **"I will never break My covenant":** Guzik reads this as God keeping his side even when Israel failed at theirs. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-2/
- **[Differing views] on whether God's promises are conditional:** Maclaren puts it differently. God's promises depend on people meeting the conditions, and a covenant God swore never to break he treats as void once people break it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_notes
- Chuck Smith takes Guzik's side: man breaks the covenant, never God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/2-3.html

**v. 2: "What is this you have done?"**
- Gill: the disobedience showed their wicked hearts, their ingratitude and their leaning toward idolatry. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-2.html
- Guzik: the question stings because there is never a good reason to disobey. He quotes Wolf: Israel's real problem was spiritual, not a lack of chariots. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-2/
- JFB: the sin was one of omission, meaning half-heartedness and neglect of duty, not some flagrant act. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_commentary
- The Biblical Illustrator agrees: no act of open rebellion is charged, only failing to obey. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/2-3.html
- TGC: this verse explains the military failures of chapter 1. They disobeyed God's commands. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/judges/

**v. 3: Thorns and a snare**
- Guzik: God let the conquest stay unfinished as a way of correcting Israel. He never meant to do all the fighting himself. This had already been warned of in Numbers 33:55. Application: Christian growth usually means working alongside God, not waiting for sin to vanish overnight. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-2/
- Ralph Davis: Israel lost the help promised in 1:2, and the main danger would be spiritual. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_commentary

**v. 4: The people wept**
- Guzik: the tears looked hopeful, but they never became lasting repentance. Real repentance shows in action, and you can be sorry about sin's results without being sorry for the sin. He quotes Spurgeon: one grain of faith is worth more than a gallon of tears. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-2/
- Wiersbe-style note on Precept Austin: the sorrow was about consequences and was shallow (2 Cor 7:8–11). JFB: the reform was only temporary. Spurgeon: a great preacher and a great sermon, yet it "ended in disappointment." https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_commentary
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: tears without reform are useless pain, and "Bochim" never appears again in Scripture. The Biblical Illustrator names three kinds of weepers (repentant, regretful, suffering) and puts Israel mostly in the "regretful" group. It also warns against purely emotional religion. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/2-3.html

**v. 5: Bochim and the sacrifices**
- Bochim means "weepers," a wordplay on "wept." https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/judges/
- Matthew Henry: the place got its name from this event. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/2-2.html
- **Location:** Coffman thinks the tabernacle had been moved to Bochim. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/2-2.html
- The Speaker's Commentary puts it near Shechem. Keil disagrees and argues that sacrificing where there was no sanctuary shows the speaker was the angel of the LORD, one with Jehovah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/2-3.html
- Precept Austin places it probably between Bethel and Shiloh. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_commentary
- **The sacrifices:** Guzik counts them as the right response: awareness of sin should drive us to God's appointed sacrifice, which for Christians means the cross. He quotes Trapp, who reads them as a sign of faith in Christ's merits. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-2/
- JFB adds that tears can never wash away sin. The blood of atonement is necessary. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_commentary

**vv. 6–9: Joshua's dismissal and death**
- Guzik: v. 6 shows the chapter is looking back to the time before Joshua's death. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-2/
- Maclaren: vv. 6–9 largely repeat Joshua 24:28–31. They link the two books and mark the start of a new era. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_notes
- v. 7: Maclaren notes that a nation or church tends to stay true while a strong leader lives. The generation that saw God act keeps that impression. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_notes
- Inrig: one person fully given to God can make a huge difference for good. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_commentary
- v. 8: Guzik says "servant of the LORD" is a title given only to great men such as Moses, David and the prophets. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-2/

**v. 10: A generation that did not know the LORD**
- Guzik: they had no personal relationship with God and no first-hand sense of his power. God was their parents' God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-2/
- Maclaren: we have to keep renewing our own first-hand sight of God's works. Faith that depends on a Joshua is a poor thing. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_notes
- Practical notes listed on Precept Austin: adults should model God's will for the next generation and teach it. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/judges_commentaries

**vv. 11–13: Baal and the Ashtoreths**
- TGC: vv. 12–13 give a crystal-clear definition of apostasy. "They abandoned the LORD," which is said twice, means they stopped serving and worshipping him. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/judges/
- Guzik: the Canaanites Israel let stay led them into idolatry. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-2/
- **What the gods were:** Guzik describes Baal as the god of weather and crops, whose appeal was wealth and success. Ashtoreth was the goddess of love, sex and fertility. He quotes Wolf: "Baal" also meant "husband" or "owner." Israel probably thought it was adding gods, not leaving God, but God demands exclusive worship, as a spouse does. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-2/
- Bible.org: Baal was the storm god behind the rain. Ashtoreth (Greek Astarte) was a goddess of fertility, love and war. https://bible.org/seriespage/appendix-0
- Older commentators such as Benson and Gill instead identify Baal with the sun and Ashtaroth with the moon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/2-13.htm
- **[Differing views] on the kind of sin:** Ellicott thinks it broke the *second* commandment more than the first. In his view Israel worshipped Jehovah under false symbols borrowed from the nations around them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-2.html
- Maclaren likewise thinks they added Baal alongside Jehovah rather than dropping Jehovah entirely, but that adding Baal *was* forsaking Jehovah. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_notes

**vv. 14–15: Anger, "sold," distress**
- "Sold" (Hebrew *makar*) means God handed them into their enemies' power. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-50-commentary
- Maclaren: God was angry because he loved them. It was all the more terrible because God was doing exactly what he had said and sworn. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_notes
- Guzik: this fulfils the covenant curses (Lev 26; Deut 28). God's aim was repentance, not punishment, so this is love, not hatred. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-2/
- **A distinctive claim from Guzik:** under the new covenant, God does not set his hand against believers the way he did against Israel. When things go badly for a believer, he says, it is simply that actions have consequences. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-2/

**v. 16: The LORD raised up judges**
- Precept Austin: the passage shows how moving God's pity is. Even when we bring trouble on ourselves, God steps in, and he stays faithful when we are not. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_commentary

**vv. 17–19: The cycle**
- Inrig: once the judge, the "restraining one," dies, the people slide back. Even God's kindness doesn't move them to stay faithful. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_commentary
- Guzik: Israel only really depended on God in emergencies, yet he answered their groaning with pity (v. 18). Christians have the Spirit and the new covenant, so they have no excuse to repeat this pattern. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-2/
- v. 18, "groaning": Bible.org notes that crying out doesn't necessarily mean repentance, though 1 Samuel 12 describes repentance as the usual pattern. https://bible.org/seriespage/appendix-0
- v. 18, God "repenting" (the KJV wording for "moved to pity"): Maclaren calls it a strong figure of speech. God's action changed from punishing to delivering, but both served one purpose. He also contrasts people's stubbornness in sin with God's patient discipline. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_notes

**vv. 20–21: "I will no longer drive out…"**
- George Bush: vv. 20–23 restate the angel's message in fuller form. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_commentary
- Maclaren: "the LORD said" probably means God's own decision, not a new revelation. The punishment fits the crime: Israel broke the covenant, so God would not keep his promise. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_notes

**v. 22: The test**
- Gill: God didn't need to find out what they would do. The test was so their sincerity, or lack of it, would show to themselves and to others. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-2.html
- Matthew Henry: "not that God might know them, but that they might know themselves." God said they couldn't resist idolatry (Deut 7:4); they thought they could. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jdg/Jdg_002.cfm
- Ellicott: mercy was mixed with the judgment. Israel had time to grow in numbers and was trained in warfare (see Judges 3:1–2). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-2.html
- Precept Austin: the Greek Old Testament uses the same word for "test" as Matthew 4:1 uses for the devil tempting Jesus. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_commentary
- Grant: it was a test, and it proved Israel rebellious. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/judges-2.html

**v. 23: Why the nations were left**
- Gill draws a spiritual parallel: God likewise lets sin remain in believers to test their faith and to show his power. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-2.html
- Constable: none of the battles in Judges are about conquering new land. They are all about throwing off an oppressor. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/2-22.html
- Precept Austin lists the reasons God left the nations: to punish (2:20), to test (2:22) and to teach Israel war (3:2). https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_2_commentary

---

**Other views**
- **Modern scholarship:** The old Catholic Encyclopedia reports Moore's critical view. On that view the body of the book, starting at 2:6, comes from the "Deuteronomistic" editors, shaped in the 7th–6th centuries BC. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08547a.htm
- Bible Odyssey groups Joshua through Kings as the "Deuteronomistic History." https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/ahab/
- **Catholic:** The same encyclopedia rejects that late dating. It suggests Samuel probably wrote the book using earlier documents. It sees 2:6–3:6 as stating the book's theme: Israel's idolatry explains why the enemy stayed and why judges were raised up. Its lesson is that when Israel leaves God, God leaves Israel "for the while," citing Augustine. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08547a.htm

**What I couldn't find (left out):** I didn't read any sources specific to the Lutheran (Kretzmann is listed but I didn't read it), Methodist or Pentecostal traditions. I also didn't find anything usable from netbible.org, Bible Odyssey on this chapter, Orthodox sites (oca.org), or on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Nothing was found for v. 9 beyond the place name.
